test_title: RRB NTPC CBT-I Official Paper (Held On: 31 Jan 2021 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Which of the following statements regarding Coriolis Force is incorrect?

options.text: It arises due to difference in atmospheric pressure.
It is maximum at the poles.
This does not happen at the equator.
It is directly proportional to the angle of latitude.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It arises due to difference in atmospheric pressure.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Coriolis Force** does not arise due to differences in atmospheric pressure.
 
• Instead, **it is caused by the rotation of the Earth, which deflects the path of moving objects (**e.g., winds, ocean currents) relative to the surface of the Earth.
 
• **Pressure differences drive winds, but the Coriolis force affects their direction.**
 
• The **Coriolis force** is **maximum at the poles** because its magnitude depends on the sine of the latitude, which is 1 at the poles.
 
• The Coriolis force is **zero at the equator** because the sine of 0° latitude is 0.
 
• The Coriolis force is **directly proportional to the sine of the latitude** (angle of latitude), making it stronger as you move from the equator toward the poles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/b5d309a4703fb6ee156ad105ab1a4035194d68085364f2cbfe08fb9b483d4cbf.png] [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Coriolis force deflects surface currents At an angle of about 45 degrees to the wind-to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern Hemisphere.
 
• It is maximum at the poles and is absent at the equator.
 
• The force acts perpendicular to the pressure gradient force.
 
• The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and the wind blows perpendicular to the isobars.
 
• Major surface ocean currents in the open ocean, however, are set in motion by the wind, which drags on the surface of the water as it blows. The winds pull surface water with them, creating currents. As these currents flow westward, the Coriolis effect, a force that results from the rotation of the Earth, deflects them.
